incidents.title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
incidents.summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, is being targeted by scammers using artificial intelligence to create fake videos and social media profiles in his name. The criminals are defrauding vulnerable immigrants by offering fraudulent services such as US residency assistance for $2,200 and claiming to help detainees escape immigration detention centers. Leal discovered the scheme when potential clients began calling his office after seeing the fake content online.

The fraud has escalated dramatically over the past three months, with an anti-piracy company hired by Leal's firm removing nearly 6,500 fake profiles, including 3,500 from TikTok, 2,400 from Facebook, and 544 from Instagram. The scams typically direct victims to contact numbers through WhatsApp, where fraudsters send phony contracts and request payment through apps like Venmo and Zelle. Leal is warning immigrants to verify service providers' identities and avoid sending money through digital payment apps, and plans to contact local and federal authorities to investigate the scams.

incidents.title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception
incidents.summary:
A fake online article featuring an invented interview between ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock highlights a growing scam trend. The fabricated piece described Bullock becoming angry during discussion of Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission reports that investment scams using deepfake images and videos of celebrities and politicians are becoming more common and sophisticated due to artificial intelligence technology.

ASIC removed 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase, including 7,051 fake investment platforms and 5,476 phishing scams. Alan Kohler, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, and wealthy individuals like Gina Rinehart appear frequently in these impersonations. Rather than using single fake images, scammers now create complex webs of deception involving fake websites, news articles, and advertisements. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing and warns that online searches alone cannot confirm legitimacy.

incidents.title: Sleep Staging Is Not Guesswork
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Oura, a smart ring company valued at $11 billion, faces a proposed class-action lawsuit filed by Clarkson Law Firm in San Francisco. The suit alleges that Oura deceived customers about its sleep tracking accuracy, claiming the company's devices cannot reliably detect the physiological signals needed to measure different sleep stages. Instead, the lawsuit contends that Oura rings rely on unreliable artificial intelligence that performs no better than random guessing. Oura markets its rings, priced at $300 and up, as capable of tracking sleep with 95% accuracy compared to clinical sleep labs, but the suit argues the devices lack the complex electrode technology that actual sleep labs use.

Oura denies the allegations, stating it stands behind its science and that its sleep staging has been validated in multiple peer-reviewed studies against polysomnography. The company notes its rings measure multiple physiological signals including heart rate and temperature. However, experts point out that consumer sleep trackers provide estimates rather than medical-grade measurements and should not be treated as substitutes for clinical sleep studies. This is not Oura's first legal challenge, as the company faces another ongoing class-action lawsuit regarding unauthorized personal data collection.

incidents.title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team discovered that the Aurora ransomware group has been active since April 2026 and is targeting organizations across multiple countries. The group operates a data leak site and has developed a Linux ransomware variant specifically designed to attack ESXi virtualization environments. Between April and May 2026, Aurora operators used Cursor Agent, an AI tool running Claude Sonnet, to conduct hands-on exploitation attacks against ten target organizations. The ESXi ransomware uses ChaCha20 encryption and includes specialized features to kill running virtual machines, encrypt virtual disk files, and leave the hypervisor bootable so victims can read ransom demands.

In a separate discovery, researchers identified a second Aurora operation cluster with medium confidence, affecting eight victim organizations across multiple countries including Israel, Germany, Austria, Spain, the United States, and Argentina. This cluster used different attack methods, including exploiting SQL Server vulnerabilities and extracting data to self-hosted storage. Gambit Security published technical indicators and command-line details of the Aurora encryptor to help organizations identify and defend against these threats.

incidents.title: A Pizza Hut franchisee is suing over a forced AI system it says wrecked deliveries
incidents.summary:
A major Pizza Hut franchisee filed a lawsuit in Texas claiming that the chain's new AI-powered delivery management system, called Dragontail, caused over $100 million in damages to its business. Chaac Pizza Northeast operates about 111 Pizza Hut locations across the Northeast and says the system created operational problems after it gave DoorDash drivers real-time visibility into kitchen workflows. The drivers began batching orders together and waiting up to fifteen minutes for additional deliveries, which meant pizzas sat longer before leaving for delivery, disappointing customers and causing sales to decline significantly.

Before the system rolled out in 2024, Chaac achieved over 90% on-time pizza delivery and double-digit sales growth. After implementation, the company experienced sharp performance drops, with New York City sales falling from positive 10% growth to negative 10% year-over-year. The lawsuit claims Pizza Hut failed to properly train operators, refused support requests, and ignored worsening metrics. Pizza Hut stated it would respond through legal channels but offered no further comment. The company faces broader challenges, with its parent company planning to close 250 U.S. locations this year.

incidents.title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Scammers have been sending personalized emails to authors, entertainers, and public figures impersonating Terry Gross and claiming to offer interview opportunities on the NPR show "Fresh Air." The fraudulent messages include detailed references to the targets' work and appear to come from legitimate production staff. However, the scam eventually requests payment of fees like $250 for so-called production costs. Misericordia University history professor Jennifer Black received such an email and initially felt flattered by the invitation, but became suspicious when the email appeared to come directly from Gross herself and contained language that seemed AI-generated. She confirmed her suspicions when asked to pay money.

WHYY, NPR, and law enforcement are investigating these fraudulent emails, which have also targeted other celebrities including comedians Nikki Glaser and Amy Poehler. Experts note that artificial intelligence has made impersonation scams more sophisticated and personalized than traditional mass-email schemes. WHYY has clarified that it never charges guests for interviews. Red flags include payment requests and the unusual situation of a major show's host personally handling interview logistics. People should verify suspicious requests by contacting organizations directly through legitimate contact information.

incidents.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Israel established a fake American think tank called the Hanover Institute for Public Policy and funded it to produce pro-Israel propaganda aimed at influencing artificial intelligence chatbots. Between August 6 and 14, the site published 124 reports totaling over 560,000 words, designed to frame Israel's position on topics like Palestinian prisoner torture, war crimes, and Gaza starvation as neutral research. The reports were formatted to resemble academic work with citations, but consistently presented information in ways that undermined criticism of Israel. The operation was part of a broader, multimillion-dollar Israeli government campaign to manipulate AI systems.

The effort involved tens of millions of dollars routed through the European advertising company Havas Media to multiple American contractors, including Clock Tower X run by former Trump strategist Brad Parscale. Researchers found the Hanover Institute site was built using platforms designed to optimize content for AI citation and training data repositories. Israeli officials have privately expressed doubts about whether such campaigns can overcome the underlying political factors affecting American public opinion, with recent polling showing declining American support for Israel, particularly among younger voters and Democrats.

Major record labels including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, and others have filed separate lawsuits against Udio and Suno, two popular artificial intelligence music generators. The labels accuse both companies of illegally copying thousands of copyrighted songs without permission to train their AI models. The lawsuits argue that the companies deliberately concealed what music they used for training and that their business model is fundamentally based on copyright infringement.

As evidence, the record labels demonstrated they could recreate famous songs by using specific prompts in both AI generators. They submitted examples showing the AI outputs closely mirrored songs by artists including The Beatles, Frank Sinatra, Chuck Berry, Mariah Carey, and Green Day. The labels provided a thumb drive of AI-generated music allegedly copying originals and submitted a list of thousands of specific copyrighted works they claim were scraped. The companies are being sued in New York and Massachusetts, and the case will establish important legal precedent for how generative AI services must handle copyright protection.

incidents.title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Lawyers representing State Farm in a Los Angeles lawsuit have apologized for using artificial intelligence that generated fake legal cases, nonexistent quotes, and false legal holdings in their court filings. The case involves homeowner Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, who sued State Farm and others after a 2020 fire in her Carson home left it uninhabitable. While repairs were underway, a storm caused water damage, and Meni-Siliga claims State Farm delayed approving repairs, ultimately leading her family to lose their home to foreclosure and declare bankruptcy. State Farm attorney Jacquelene Robinson admitted that seven case citations across eight filings did not exist, and she incorrectly thought an AI tool called Irys was connected to her law firm's legal research subscription.

The use of AI in law has become widespread, with 41 percent of law firms and 47 percent of corporate legal departments using generative AI. A worldwide database has documented 1,922 cases of AI-generated legal hallucinations, with most occurring in the United States. A California attorney was previously fined a record ten thousand dollars for using ChatGPT in a brief containing 21 made-up quotes. Meni-Siliga's case is scheduled to go to trial in October.

stories.Summary:
# Summary

China's data industry reached 6.78 trillion yuan in 2025, and the country is now focusing on coordinating development between its data sector and artificial intelligence capabilities. The 2026 China International Big Data Industry Expo, held in Guiyang from August 28-30, attracted 372 companies and over 16,000 guests to showcase innovations in computing power, large models, and data circulation. Government officials emphasized that high-quality datasets are essential for advancing AI capabilities and that data technology is transforming traditional industries like power generation and renewable energy forecasting.

Beyond upgrading existing industries, data and AI are creating new business opportunities and employment categories. Companies are hiring data collectors to train robots through embodied intelligence projects, while micro-enterprises and one-person startups are emerging as signs of entrepreneurial growth. International participants from Zimbabwe, Chile, Pakistan, and other nations attended to explore cooperation opportunities, with officials highlighting the potential for shared benefits and technological exchange between countries through collaborative data and AI development.

stories.Headline: Who Writes AI's Rules When Someone Else Owns the Machines?
stories.Summary:
# Summary

South Africa withdrew its Draft National AI Policy in April 2026 after discovering that at least six of its 67 academic references were fabricated, highlighting a broader challenge facing the Global South. The incident underscores a critical debate about who controls artificial intelligence governance and infrastructure. Currently, the United States and China host roughly 86% of global data centre capacity, giving them power to set rules and prices for AI systems worldwide. This concentration of computing power represents what critics call "tech colonialism," where developing nations provide data and demand but lack ownership and control over the technology itself.

BRICS countries and other Global South nations are attempting to shift AI governance away from Western-led standards by emphasizing digital sovereignty and development rights. They are seeking to anchor AI governance within the United Nations rather than OECD-led bodies and have established organizations like the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation. However, meaningful sovereignty requires owning physical infrastructure, not just adopting policies. The article notes that until developing nations build regional computing capacity and chip manufacturing capabilities, they remain dependent on foreign platforms controlled by American hyperscalers or Chinese firms. True sovereignty means choosing dependencies rather than having them imposed.

stories.Headline: CSA's Top Cloud Threats: Identity, AI -- Campus Technology
stories.Summary:
The Cloud Security Alliance surveyed 507 security professionals to identify the top threats to cloud computing in 2026. Identity and access management issues rose to the number one concern, moving up from second place in 2024, while misconfiguration dropped to fifth. Two artificial intelligence-related threats appeared in the rankings for the first time, including AI-enhanced attacks and AI system compromise. The top eleven threats also include insecure third-party resources, insecure APIs, advanced persistent threats, and inadequate cloud security strategy and governance.

The survey results reveal a significant shift in the cloud threat landscape, with organizations now prioritizing identity protection, artificial intelligence risks, and software supply chains over infrastructure-focused concerns. Security scores ranged closely from 7.95 for identity and access management to 7.45 for system vulnerabilities. The report aims to help organizations make informed risk-management decisions about cloud adoption by providing expert analysis of technical and business impacts, real-world examples, and corresponding security controls across cloud and AI environments.

While many investors focus on chip designers like Nvidia and AMD, the author contends that Taiwan Semiconductor holds the real advantage because it manufactures chips for these companies and controls approximately 72 percent of the global foundry market. Taiwan Semiconductor benefits from a neutral position in the competition between chip designers, meaning it will profit regardless of which company's hardware becomes dominant. The company's CEO expects elevated demand for chips to continue through at least 2029 or 2030, providing several more years of strong growth. Additionally, Taiwan Semiconductor plans to launch new chip technology that will allow for price increases, positioning it as one of the safest investments in the artificial intelligence sector.
